item.description:
• Packages. A new tile on Home opens curated roads by area: the Eifel, the French Alps, the Swiss Alps and the Bergisches Land, each a card with its story and its roads. The Eifel has four loops from about 40 minutes to an afternoon; the Bergisches Land ten hill repeats from one minute to eight, every one in Apple's photographic 3D; every loop says how long it takes you. Real roads read to the metre, free during the beta and yours to keep. The list is fetched when you open the page, and nothing about you is sent. Install adds a pack's roads to your library; Remove puts them in the Trash and keeps your rides.
  • Hill repeats show the climb. The panel at the top left now draws this climb from foot to top, coloured by gradient, with you on it. Between climbs it shows the next one, so you can see what is coming. Every climb you have ridden races you as a numbered ghost, on the road and on the profile: you on top, then the fastest climb, down to the slowest — so the tenth climb can be held against the first, not only the ninth. The panel says how you stand against the last climb and the first.
  • Steep hills say so. A road whose steepest stretch is over 12% carries a "Steep" tag — on My roads, in Explore, on a pack's road once installed and on the start line — with the FTP it takes to keep 60 rpm in the easiest gear. If yours is below it, the tag says what it needs, in orange. The road still rides; it is a hint, not a lock.

• Choose a road on the map. The + on Home's road slot opens Explore: every road on the map, and filters for what you want from the ride — what its climbs are good for (VO₂max, threshold, a long climb, steady endurance), how long it takes you, how big its biggest climb is (Strava's categories), ridden or not yet, and the kind of road. Each choice says how many roads it would leave. Times and climbs are worked out for your FTP and weight. Pick a road, then Choose.
  • Import a GPX from Explore. Import GPX… at the top of Explore, or drop a file anywhere on it: the road is brought in as on My roads, asked about streets and heights the same way, and the map flies to it.
  • Right-click a road in Explore's list to ride (or choose) it, show it on the map, look at it in 3D, show its original file, or move one of your own roads to the Trash — with its original file, as on My roads. Its rides stay.
  • Looking up streets and heights shows how far it has got. A bar counts the road's map squares as OpenStreetMap and the laser survey answer, with the seconds on the one being asked — and when OpenStreetMap's server is busy or down it says so ("not answering (502) — asking again in 20 s, try 3 of 5"). A server that is down now gives up after one round of tries instead of three, and Try again asks once more.

• Explore: every road on one map. A new page (⌘8) shows all your roads on the satellite map from above, coloured by their steepness as in the ride — or by whether you have ridden them, or by kind. Point at one to see its length, climbing, its climbs, where its heights came from and how often you have ridden it; click it for its profile, a look along it in 3D, or Ride. The list beside the map shows the roads in view first, with search and filters.
  • Gears back when the workout is done. A workout on a road used to hold you at an easy ERG wattage once it had finished, in whatever gear the last block left. Now the ride goes over to the road and your gears at once, in an easy gear, so you can ride on and shift as you like.
  • A ride's summary tells the road. After a ride on a road — a pass, your own road, or a workout on one — the summary shows what you rode in 3D on the satellite map (drag, pinch and turn to look around), the profile in the gradient's colours, where you started and finished, distance, metres climbed and descended, the highest point and the steepest ramp, and every climb with its time, VAM, watts, heart rate and cadence. The top of the summary is new too: time, distance, climbing, speed, watts and TSS at a glance, the rest grouped by effort, heart and legs. Rides from before keep their summary as it was.
